variants.name: Typed AbortSignal threaded through interfaces + awaited completion
variants.idiom_name: AbortSignal option + await the worker's promise
variants.implementation_notes: TypeScript adds no runtime facility to the JavaScript story, so the pattern is typed rather than implemented: AbortSignal becomes part of the worker's options interface (every method that can block takes { signal }: AbortSignal), abort() is phase 1, and awaiting the worker's promise is phase 2 with cleanup in finally. The type system's contribution is contractual - signal threaded through every collaborator means a caller cannot forget the cancellation channel, and the completion is typed as Promise<void> so the controller must await it. Hand-rolled boolean flags remain for code that predates the DOM/Node typings, but they lose exactly this contract.
pitfalls: AbortSignal is single-use: after abort it stays aborted, so a restart needs a new controller; passing a stale signal to a new worker makes its first awaited call reject immediately.
`signal` must be threaded into every blocking collaborator (fetch, database clients, timers); a signal that stops at the interface boundary cancels nothing.

Dom and Node AbortSignal types differ in places (lib.dom vs @types/node), so the same code can fail to typecheck in the server build; keep the signal type in the shared options type and let each side import its own definition.
Node does not wait for pending promises at process exit: the controller must await the worker promise before returning from the shutdown path.

variants.name: Typed worker_threads shutdown message + 'exit'
variants.implementation_notes: When the participant is a real worker thread, TypeScript's contribution is the message contract: a discriminated union of control messages makes the shutdown request one arm of the protocol, so it cannot be confused with data messages, and once(worker, 'exit') is the typed completion step. worker.terminate() stays the forced fallback (it stops JavaScript execution as soon as possible and skips in-worker cleanup). Pair it with AbortSignal inside the worker for the work it is doing.
pitfalls: The 'exit' event also fires for a crash or an early process.exit: make the worker acknowledge that its flush completed (or flush synchronously) instead of trusting exit alone.
Message ordering gives no back-pressure: a shutdown message can arrive while a data message is still being processed, so the handler must define whether the current item is finished or abandoned.

worker.terminate() is not a graceful stop - it stops all JavaScript execution as soon as possible and returns only at 'exit', so a caller that uses it as the normal path loses the second phase entirely.
